source: CAMFAD student thesis: "Establishment of a New Coconut Plantation Farm", National School of Agriculture, July 1994. Note: this source states harvest 'normally begins when the palm reaches about 3 years of age', which is notably earlier than the 5-7 years to first bearing stated in the AIDOC farmer leaflet in this knowledge base (see coconut/intro_lifespan_uses) -- reported here as printed rather than silently reconciled; it may reflect an early/precocious variety, a different definition of 'harvest start', or a transcription/printing issue in the source.
text:
Harvest timing: the thesis states harvest normally begins once the palm is about 3 years old (see the sourcing note on this figure above). Two types of harvesting tools are described: Tool (A), usable for about 10 years before replacement; and Tool (B), also used for harvesting, illustrated in the source alongside a long-handled digging/scraping tool and a curved blade tool, plus an illustration of a harvester climbing/reaching a palm with a long pole tool to cut down a fruit bunch.

Harvest technique: leaves should not be cut when harvesting fruit bunches, since removing leaves can reduce future yield. Ripeness is judged by the bunch itself: farmers can tell a bunch is ready to harvest once 2-3 nuts from that bunch have already fallen naturally to the ground, taken as a sign the remaining nuts in the bunch are also mature.

Productive lifespan: although a coconut palm can live over 60 years, the thesis notes that plantations are typically renewed/replanted after about 25-30 years of production, because yield declines once trees pass this age.

Yield figures given in the source (approximately 5-25 units per hectare, unit not fully legible in the scan -- likely bunches or a similar count-based measure rather than weight) are not reproduced with full confidence here due to the scan's legibility at this point in the text; a clearer copy would let a future session confirm the exact figure and unit.
